title: The suffering ummah
hook: wars, refugees and persecution today, and Muslim charities working amid them

segments.voice: Yesterday, women scholars: Aisha correcting the reporters, Karima teaching Bukhari in Mecca, women teachers today. Your line was: they always taught. Who did you thank? Today is a harder one. Day one thousand thirty-three.

Rice, lentils, oil, a blanket, soap, a small bag of dates. Volunteers in mismatched gloves are packing them into boxes in a borrowed warehouse. Someone tapes, someone labels, someone's phone keeps buzzing with news from a place most of them have never seen. The boxes are going to people who left home with what they could carry. Nobody in the warehouse can stop the war that sent them running. They can fill the next box. Today: the suffering ummah.
screen: `RICE, OIL, A BLANKET, DATES.` → `A BORROWED WAREHOUSE.` → `THEY CAN FILL THE NEXT BOX.`

segments.voice: Ummah is the word for the community of believers, all Muslims everywhere, across every border. And in our time, parts of that body are hurting badly: war, displacement, refugee camps, persecution for faith or ethnicity. This lesson won't take sides in any conflict or rank anyone's pain. It looks at one teaching, and what people do with it. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, gave a picture of how believers belong to one another. It is reported in Sahih Muslim: the believers, in their love and mercy and kindness to one another, are like one body. When one part of it aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever. Not sympathy from a distance. Fever. That picture is why the news from one corner of the world can keep someone awake on the other side of it. And the picture asks for more than feeling. Across the Muslim world and in Muslim communities elsewhere, it has been turned into work: zakat committees, mosque food drives, large charities that run clinics, wells and shelters in war zones and after disasters, often alongside the Red Crescent and many others. Some of these charities say they help anyone in need, whatever their faith. The Qur'an puts the instruction plainly: "Help ye one another unto righteousness and pious duty." The body feels the pain. Then it does the next small thing.
screen: `UMMAH: ALL THE BELIEVERS.` · `ONE BODY: WHEN ONE PART ACHES.` · `FEVER BECOMES WORK.` · `HELP YE ONE ANOTHER.` · then, large: `THE BODY FEELS THE PAIN.`

segments.voice: The practice: give to a refugee charity. First, settle, and breathe. Bring to mind people who have had to leave home: a family on a road, a child in a camp, someone waiting at a border. Don't picture anyone you can't bear to; keep it gentle. With each out-breath, hold one of them for a moment. If you pray, you can ask God's mercy for them in your own words. Then, when the bell sounds, choose one charity that serves refugees, any you trust, and give something, however small: money, time, a box of supplies. The bell holds the time.
Ummah, the worldwide community of believers that the Prophet pictured as one body, feeling fever when any part of it aches. Today's word.
Your line: the body feels the pain. Today, when the news hurts, do one small thing for someone far away, then one for someone near. Day one thousand thirty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims give zakat and voluntary charity, often through mosques and Muslim relief organizations that send food, medicine and shelter to people affected by war and disaster, and appeals are common at Friday prayers and in Ramadan.
